author: assistant sub-agent V3G1 (v3 re-map); fix pass Fix1

vectors.enisa_quote: complete replacement of a satellite's legitimate signals
vectors.reason: Weak: ENISA does not say who replaces the signal or from where; replacing a signal the satellite receives means transmitting on its radio link from outside the mission.

vectors.enisa_quote: primarily impacting the satellite control center and TTC ground stations
vectors.reason: Weak: the quote names what is impacted (control centre and TTC ground stations), not where the attacker acts; the attacker position inside the ground segment is inferred from the SLE protocol that ties those two together.

review_response.finding: S2 / whole rf_link chain disappears under SDLS (EX-0006 placed after an entry that SDLS blocks)
review_response.action: kept because: EX-0006 alters on-board encryption and counter state, which needs a command the satellite already accepted; an outsider without keys has none when SDLS is on, so the engine result is correct. ENISA's 'compromising the SDL protocol' is the assumption that SDLS is broken or absent; the report must say that SDLS-on results assume an intact protocol and that this threat is the one that breaks it. No link_only override was used.

review_response.finding: EX-0006 is the wrong carrier on the ground vector
review_response.action: fixed: EX-0006 restricted to vectors [rf_link]; IA-0007 now carries the SLE half with sparta_quote 'data gateways (SLE/CSP)' and enables the guidance-command action EX-0012.08.

review_response.finding: IMP-0008 and IMP-0011 share one quote for two things; EX-0012.08 is the better guidance-control technique
review_response.action: fixed: EX-0012.08 added as analyst_added K-ACTION with the quote 'unauthorized commands to guidance control'; IMP-0011 now quotes 'complete replacement of a satellite's legitimate signals'; IMP-0008 is kept (prior decision, and other threats drop to it) with its own quote and a reason that flags it as the weakest effect row.

review_response.finding: IMP-0011 K-ACTION here but K-EFFECT in TR52/TR54/TR44
review_response.action: fixed: K-EFFECT impact; the sending is done by the K-ENABLE entry rows (IA-0007.02, IA-0008.x).
fixed: K-ENABLE role entry here, same as TR51, TR52 and TR57.

review_response.finding: 'replacement of a satellite's legitimate signals' as downlink or transponder replacement has no kept step
review_response.action: kept because: no SPARTA technique replaces a downlink signal without a command (EXF-0006.02 Transponder diverts data for collection); reported as ENISA text not fully covered, no sparta_gap on the whole threat since commands and protocol compromise are covered.

review_response.finding: DE-0003.07 Cryptographic Modes as a companion of EX-0006 (review, optional)
review_response.action: kept because: EX-0006 already carries 'forcing algorithm fallbacks' and 'null ciphers'; DE-0003.07 is a concealment technique, so it stays D-UNDESCRIBED.

review_response.finding: rf_link quote, IMP-0007, DE-0004/EX-0001.01/EX-0014.x to TR54, DE-0002.02/EX-0016.x to TR44, PER-0004 to TR52, RD-0001.01 (no issue)
review_response.action: kept because: confirmed in the review; rf_link basis changed to weak because the quote names the signals, not the attacker's position.

review_response.finding: fix pass: validator, EX-0012.08 and IMP-0011 kept for rf_link but every enabler belonged to ground
review_response.action: fixed: IA-0008 and IA-0008.01 now enable EX-0006, EX-0012.08 and IMP-0011, so the rf_link vector has its own enablers for each step; ground keeps IA-0007 -> EX-0012.08 and IA-0007.02 -> IMP-0011.

review_response.finding: fix pass M7: ground vector basis 'quote' overstated
review_response.action: fixed: basis weak; the quote names what is impacted, not the attacker's position (same standard as rf_link).

review_response.finding: fix pass M5: caveats promised in earlier responses were not in the file
review_response.action: fixed: notes array added (SDLS-on assumes an intact protocol; downlink/transponder replacement uncovered).

review_response.finding: fix pass M3/m3: IMP-0008 quote overlaps EX-0012.08; no edge from EX-0006 to the outcomes
review_response.action: kept because the outcomes follow any accepted entry (each entry now enables them) and the overlapping quote is ENISA's only wording for the guidance-control effect; the reason already flags IMP-0008 as the weakest row. Process commentary removed from the reasons.

rows.enisa_quote: compromising the SLE and SDL protocols
rows.sparta_quote: traffic or data is processed in clear or with weakened protection
rows.reason: For the outside transmitter the SDL half of 'compromising the SLE and SDL protocols' is defeating link protection (null ciphers, skipped anti-replay checks); limited to rf_link because a ground insider already holds the keys.

rows.sparta_quote: Editing these values skews estimation or control
rows.reason: Guidance control is the attitude determination and control subsystem; unauthorized commands there edit its estimator and controller values, which is a concrete action behind ENISA's phrase.

ENISA puts the hijack at the control centre and TTC ground stations and at the SLE protocol; IA-0007 names the SLE/CSP data gateways as part of the ground system whose compromise gives the foothold for the guidance commands.

rows.sparta_quote: Adversaries may use a compromised, mission-owned ground system to transmit legitimate-looking commands to the target spacecraft
rows.reason: The compromised control centre or TTC station sends the unauthorized commands that ENISA says hijack the satellite.

rows.sparta_quote: Most interact by radiating or exchanging traffic using mission-compatible waveforms, framing, or crosslink protocols
rows.reason: An external transmitter that radiates mission-compatible signals is what can replace the legitimate signal, and it must first defeat the link protection.

rows.sparta_quote: Adversaries may field their own ground system, transportable or fixed, to transmit and receive mission-compatible signals
rows.reason: A rogue ground station is the concrete transmitter that substitutes its own signals for the legitimate ones.

rows.enisa_quote: complete replacement of a satellite's legitimate signals
rows.sparta_quote: An adversary may inject an unauthorized command or alter a legitimate command before execution
rows.reason: Replacing the legitimate signal means attacker-controlled commands or data flow to the satellite in its place; the sending is done by the entry rows.

rows.enisa_quote: Hijacking and unauthorized commands to guidance control
rows.sparta_quote: An adversary may force an unauthorized transition
rows.reason: Hijacking means the attacker decides the operating state and mode; this is the weakest effect row, because ENISA names commands to a subsystem, not a mode change.

rows.sparta_quote: The function may operate exactly as designed, but the adversary uses it for an unauthorized or harmful purpose
rows.reason: Using the satellite's own functions for the attacker's purpose is the stated aim of the hijack.
Fielding a rogue ground station needs its own ground station equipment.
Valid unauthorized commands need the mission's command formats and dictionaries.
Inhibiting ground-system functions (hiding activity from operators) is concealment; ENISA's hijack describes taking over signals and commands, not hiding them.
Overpowering the link by jamming is denial of service; ENISA's hijack replaces or alters the signal instead of drowning it, and TR44 keeps this technique.
Switching crypto modes or 'crypto off' states is a way to desynchronise or hide traffic; EX-0006 already carries the protocol-weakening ENISA names, and ENISA mentions no hidden-content step.
Biasing the system clock to evade detection is concealment through timing; the hijack text mentions no clock manipulation.
Corrupting GPS ephemeris to hide activity is a navigation-side evasion that the hijack text does not describe.
Presenting as an authorised origin is the spoofing threat (a signal that appears legitimate); TR54 keeps it, whereas hijacking here is described through protocol compromise.
Deceiving onboard space-domain-awareness sensors targets SSA payloads, which ENISA's hijack of the signals and guidance commands does not name.
Replay of captured traffic is not mentioned; ENISA speaks of altering or replacing signals and unauthorized commands, and replay as such belongs to the sub-technique TR54 keeps.
Resending previously accepted telecommands is a spoofing means kept by TR54; ENISA hijacking does not mention captured commands.
Replaying bus traffic acts inside the spacecraft network; ENISA's text is about the radio signals and the ground protocols.
PNT geofencing makes behaviour depend on position; nothing in the hijack text suggests location-triggered execution.
Time-synchronised execution schedules actions for later; ENISA describes the hijack, not delayed or timed payload actions.
Relative time sequences chain actions after an event; the hijack text names no timing of commands.
Editing internal routing tables redirects on-board data; ENISA's hijack is about signals and guidance commands, not on-board routing.
Editing the system clock skews timing; the hijack text does not mention time.
Erroneous input exhausts receivers and parsers (a denial effect); ENISA's hijack is about taking over, not about overloading.
Forging inputs that look trustworthy is the spoofing threat, which TR54 keeps; the hijack text describes replacing the signal through protocol compromise.
Time spoofing forges the time source seen by consumers; ENISA hijacking names no time attack, and spoofing in general belongs to TR54.
Spoofing bus messages acts on internal networks; the hijack text is about the radio signals and the SLE/SDL protocols.
Fabricated sensor measurements are the spoofing threat; TR54 keeps this technique and the hijack text names no sensor data.
Transmitting false navigation signals is the spoofing threat, kept by TR54; the hijack text says nothing about GNSS.
Jamming is the denial threat kept by TR44; replacing a signal is the opposite of drowning it.
Uplink jamming prevents acceptance of telecommands (TR44 and TR32 threat); the hijack wants the satellite to accept the attacker's commands.
Downlink jamming blocks telemetry and is part of the jamming threat TR44 keeps, not of a signal takeover.
Jamming navigation or timing signals denies GNSS; the hijack text names no navigation service.
Replaying data to exfiltrate it is a collection step; ENISA's hijack states no data theft.
Traffic-analysis exfiltration infers information from link patterns; hijacking states no information gain.
Timing side channels leak information passively; the hijack text describes active takeover.
Signal interception is the eavesdropping threat kept by TR29; the hijack text describes altering or replacing signals, not listening.
Intercepting the uplink to read commands is part of TR29's interception threat; ENISA's hijack sends commands rather than reads them.
Intercepting the downlink is the interception threat TR29 keeps; not an action of a hijack.
An out-of-band link to move data out is exfiltration; ENISA hijacking names no data leaving the system.

Remapping the transponder to favour non-mission receivers diverts data to the attacker; this is signal diversion for collection, and ENISA names reuse of the satellite, not data diversion (accepted as a gap for the 'replacement of signals' sentence).
Using a compromised ground system as an exfiltration path is the ground-compromise threat TR38 keeps; ENISA's hijack names no data theft.
Exfiltration from a partner site is not part of the hijack; no partner is named.
Exfiltration over the payload communication channel is an on-board implant behaviour kept by TR46, not a hijack action.
Supply-chain compromise before launch is not described; ENISA's hijack is of an operating satellite's signals and ground protocols.
Poisoned development tools and dependencies are a supply-chain route that the hijack text does not mention.
Software supply-chain compromise is the supply-chain threat kept by TR55; ENISA hijacking names protocol compromise instead.
Tampered hardware from the supply chain is not described for a hijack of signals.
Compromising the satellite's software-defined radio changes the on-board receiver itself; ENISA's text puts the compromise in the SLE/SDL protocols and the ground, not the SDR (not named).
Entering through a compromised neighbour satellite is a crosslink route; ENISA mentions only ground and bus.
A secondary or backup comm channel as the door is not named; the hijack text names the standard SLE/SDL path.
Using a backup ground station is a different door than the primary control centre and TTC stations ENISA names.
A secondary receiver as a way in is not named; ENISA gives the main link and the ground protocols.
Rendezvous and proximity operations are not described; the hijack is described over signals and ground protocols.
Compromise emanations is passive side-channel eavesdropping; a hijack needs to act, not listen.
A docked vehicle or OSAM servicer is a physical-contact route the hijack text does not mention.
Grappling the satellite is physical capture, not the signal replacement or command abuse ENISA describes.
Compromising a hosted payload as a door into the bus is not described; ENISA names the bus itself as the space target.
Compromising an on-orbit update pushes malicious software; ENISA's hijack is through protocol compromise, and TR46 keeps the update route.
A rogue spacecraft is a proximity origin; ENISA points to ground stations and the link, not to a neighbouring vehicle.
A counterspace weapon as the origin is the ASAT threat TR18 keeps; the hijack text does not name one.
A trusted relationship as the way in is not named in the hijack text.
A mission collaborator as the origin is not named; ENISA places the threat at the control centre and TTC stations.
A vendor's remote access is not named for the hijack; supply chain and vendors are not mentioned.
Hijacking via the user segment is not described: ENISA names no user terminal or service link (the user-terminal origin is not chosen).
Entering during safe mode relies on reduced protections; the hijack text does not mention safe mode.
Auxiliary devices and removable media are a different access route that the hijack text does not mention.
Assembly, test and launch compromise happens before launch; ENISA's hijack is of an operating satellite.
Moving from a compromised bus into a hosted RAN function is not described by ENISA.
Altering stored settings is the parameter-modification threat TR57 keeps; the hijack text names signals and commands.
Falsifying data content is the data-manipulation threat TR39 keeps; the hijack text is about signals and commands.
Changing executable code is the software-modification threat TR42 keeps; ENISA hijacking names protocol compromise, not a code change.
Depleting or monopolising a resource is resource exhaustion kept by TR51; hijacking aims at reuse, not denial.
Manipulating the time reference is a timing effect; the hijack text names no clock or synchronisation outcome.
Moving from the bus into a hosted payload is a lateral step that the hijacking text does not describe.
Exploiting missing bus segregation moves between subsystems; ENISA names bus and ground but no internal movement.
Hopping to other satellites over crosslinks is constellation movement; the hijack text covers a single satellite.
A rideshare payload as a lateral path is not described for the hijack.
Keeping a presence in the ground system is persistence, which ENISA does not state for the hijack.
Replacing cryptographic keys to lock users out is the seizure-of-control outcome that TR52 keeps; the hijack text does not describe lockout.
Preparing compromised infrastructure is not needed by a kept row of this chain.
Compromising a mission-operated ground system is resource preparation; IA-0007 is the kept step, and no kept row depends on this one.
Compromising a third-party ground system is preparation for a different origin; no kept row depends on it.
Obtaining cryptographic keys is a preparation step for key abuse; no kept row of this chain needs keys, since EX-0006 weakens the protection instead.
Staging capabilities is generic preparation that no kept row of this chain depends on.
Staging an exploit or payload for upload serves code injection, not the protocol compromise ENISA names.
Learning the cryptographic algorithms is reconnaissance for attacking crypto; ENISA says the protocols are compromised but no kept row needs this knowledge as a preparation.
Gathering general spacecraft communication details is not needed beyond the command formats that REC-0003.02 supplies.
Scanning for the mission's channel serves a jammer; the rogue ground station here already knows its target (RD-0001.01 covers the equipment).
Collecting valid credentials is reconnaissance for credential misuse; the hijack text does not describe stolen credentials.
Eavesdropping as reconnaissance is not needed by a kept row; command formats come from REC-0003.02.
Intercepting the uplink to learn commands is not needed by the kept rows and is not named by ENISA.
Intercepting the downlink is not needed by any kept row of the hijack chain.
Active RF or optical scanning of the target is not needed by a kept row; the hijack text mentions no probing.
Watching for safe-mode indicators prepares access during safe mode, which the hijack text does not describe.

notes: SDLS-on results assume an intact protocol: this threat is the one ENISA describes as breaking the SLE/SDL protocols, so a SDLS-on scenario that stops the rf_link chain describes an uncompromised protocol, not the threat's own case.

Not covered: ENISA's 'complete replacement of a satellite's legitimate signals' on the downlink or transponder has no SPARTA technique that works without an accepted command (EXF-0006.02 diverts data for collection, which is another outcome).
